findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order()` is added as a non-default method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI interface in `keycloak-common`. Any implementation that lives outside this repository (keycloak-client repo, adapter/distribution forks, custom FIPS integrations) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` sorts the loaded providers by `order()`. Since the whole point of the change is to allow extra providers to coexist, this should be declared as a `default` method (e.g. returning the current 200 baseline) so existing implementations remain binary- and source-compatible.

findings.title: Silently picking a provider when several share the same order hides classpath misconfiguration
findings.body: The previous code threw `IllegalStateException("Multiple crypto providers loaded ... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath")`. It is now replaced by a debug-level log and `foundProviders.get(0)` is used. All three in-tree providers return `order() == 200` (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`), so when two of them end up on the classpath the winner is decided by `ServiceLoader` iteration order, i.e. by classpath ordering, which is not deterministic across environments. In a FIPS deployment where both `keycloak-crypto-fips1402` and `keycloak-crypto-default` are present, this can silently select the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider instead of failing loudly, producing a non-compliant installation that is very hard to diagnose. Either keep a hard failure for ties in `order()`, or give the providers distinct orders (fips > default) and log the ignored ones at WARN.

findings.title: Test uses a P-256 key for all algorithms and never validates the produced DER
findings.body: The key pair is created with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (default curve, P-256) and reused for ES256, ES384 and ES512. Consequently r/s are always 32 significant bytes, and after padding to 48/66 bytes the re-encoded DER sequence stays below 128 bytes, so `ASN1Encoder.writeLength()`'s long-form branch (`length > 127`) and the decoder's multi-byte length branch are never exercised – exactly the paths that real P-521/ES512 signatures hit. In addition the test only asserts that `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x`, i.e. the new encoder is only checked against the new decoder; a malformed DER output would still round-trip and pass. The test should generate keys with `ECGenParameterSpec("secp256r1"/"secp384r1"/"secp521r1")` matching each algorithm and verify the generated DER with `Signature.verify()` (and/or compare it byte-wise with the signature produced by the JDK).

findings.title: Indefinite-length / empty encodings cause unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
findings.body: `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but no caller handles that value: `readInteger()` passes it to `read(length)` which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws `NegativeArraySizeException`, and `readNext()` computes a bogus length. Similarly, a zero-length INTEGER makes `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throw `NumberFormatException`. These are unchecked exceptions escaping methods declared to throw `IOException`, so callers of `ECDSACryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS()` that only catch `IOException` will propagate a runtime exception for malformed input. Reject indefinite length (and empty integer content) with an `IOException` instead.

findings.title: Dead no-op statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write `rBigInteger`/`sBigInteger` into them and discard the results; the actual DER is built again on lines 117-121. These statements have no effect other than extra allocations and they suggest to a reader that something is being accumulated into shared state. They should be removed.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically `SUN`/`SunJSSE`, which is not a BouncyCastle provider as the interface documents ("BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider"). `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this value and is used throughout keycloak-core as the provider name for `Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)`, `KeyStore.getInstance("BCFKS", PROVIDER)`, `Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding", PROVIDER)`, etc. With this provider selected, those calls will silently be routed to the JDK provider and fail with a confusing `NoSuchAlgorithmException` for BC-only algorithms. If no BC provider is available, either return `null` (as `WildFlyElytronProvider` does) or throw a descriptive `UnsupportedOperationException` explaining that BouncyCastle is not on the classpath.
